source_text: Wilberforce: “I confess to you sir, so enormous so dreadful, so irremediable [impossible to fix] did its wickedness appear that my own mind was completely made up for the abolition. A trade founded in iniquity [wrongdoing] . . . must be abolished . . . let the consequences be what they would, I from this time determined that I would never rest till I had effected [achieved] its abolition.”  Equiano: “I now saw myself deprived [robbed] of all chance of returning to my native country . . . . I was soon put down under the decks, and there I received such a salutation [greeting] in my nostrils as I had never experienced in my life . . . . I became so sick and low that I was not able to eat . . . . I inquired [asked] of them what was to be done with us? They gave me to understand we were to be carried to these white people's country to work for them.”

model_response: In Document 8, Wilberforce tells Parliament in 1789 that he will never rest until the slave trade is abolished, and Equiano describes being carried away below deck with no chance of returning home. Their campaign worked, slowly: in 1807, Parliament abolished the British slave trade. Equiano's account was part of what changed minds, because it let British readers hear from a person who had survived the trade.
